lessons.title: Module 2 Lesson 1: Understanding Your Customer Base in African Markets
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 2 of Small Shop and Market Trading. In this first lesson we focus on the most important asset in your business: your customers. Without a clear understanding of who buys from you, why they buy, and how they behave, even the best-stocked shop will struggle. Across African markets, from Kibera to Kumasi, from Lagos to Lusaka, successful traders share one habit: they know their customers deeply. This lesson will help you build that knowledge systematically. Start by mapping your catchment area. Who lives within a 10 to 15 minute walk of your shop or stall? In many African towns and cities, most customers come from a surprisingly small radius. Walk the area. Note the housing types, the schools, the churches and mosques, the transport routes, the factories, the offices. Each of these brings different customer groups at different times. A shop near a primary school will see mothers and children in the morning and afternoon. A stall near a bus stage will see commuters early morning and evening. A shop near a construction site will see workers wanting quick, filling food and phone credit. Write down what you observe. Use a simple notebook or your phone notes. Do not rely on memory alone. Next, segment your customers. Segmentation simply means grouping customers by shared needs. Common segments in African small trade include: daily wage earners who buy small quantities frequently; households buying weekly or monthly in bulk; students buying snacks, airtime, and stationery; travellers buying water, biscuits, and phone credit; and institutions such as schools, clinics, or offices buying in larger volumes. Each segment has different price sensitivity, different shopping times, and different product preferences. For each segment, ask: what problem are they solving when they come to me? A worker buying bread and tea at 6am is solving hunger and time pressure. A mother buying soap and maize flour is solving household provisioning. A student buying airtime is solving connectivity and social belonging. When you understand the problem, you can stock and price accordingly. Now consider purchasing power and payment behaviour. In many African markets, cash remains king, but mobile money is rapidly changing how people pay. If you are in Kenya, M-Pesa is almost universal. In Ghana, MTN Mobile Money and Vodafone Cash are common. In Nigeria, bank transfers and USSD payments are widespread. In Francophone West Africa, Orange Money and Wave are growing. Accepting mobile money can increase sales because customers do not need to carry cash, and it reduces your risk of theft. However, you must factor in transaction fees and the time to confirm payments. Train yourself and any staff to confirm payments before releasing goods. Also consider credit. Many small shops in Africa extend informal credit, known as book or ledger credit. This can build loyalty, but it can also destroy your cash flow if not managed. If you offer credit, set clear rules: who qualifies, what the limit is, when repayment is due, and what happens if they do not pay. Keep a simple credit book with names, amounts, dates, and balances. Do not let credit exceed what you can afford to lose. Another key area is understanding customer frequency and basket size. Frequency is how often a customer visits. Basket size is how much they spend per visit. Some shops have high frequency and low basket size, such as a kiosk selling single cigarettes, sweets, and airtime. Others have low frequency and high basket size, such as a shop selling building materials. Your location, stock, and pricing determine which model you operate. You can grow by increasing frequency, increasing basket size, or both. To increase frequency, make your shop convenient, well-stocked, and friendly. To increase basket size, use bundling, upselling, and strategic placement. For example, place bread next to milk, or put airtime near the counter where customers queue. In African markets, relationships matter enormously. Customers often buy from people they trust and who treat them with respect. Greet every customer. Learn names. Remember what they usually buy. If a customer buys the same brand of tea every week, have it ready. If a customer is short of cash today, a kind word and a small flexibility can earn loyalty for years. But do not confuse relationship with poor business discipline. Be warm and be firm. Set prices clearly. Use a price list or labels so there is no argument. If you must change prices due to inflation or supply costs, explain why and do it consistently for everyone. Fairness builds trust. Now let us talk about competition. In most African markets, you are not alone. There may be several shops selling similar goods within a short distance. Do not compete only on price, because that destroys your margins. Instead, compete on reliability, cleanliness, opening hours, friendliness, and product mix. If your competitor runs out of cooking oil every month, you can win customers by always having it. If your competitor closes at 6pm, you can stay open until 8pm for commuters. If your competitor is rude, you can be welcoming. Small differences create big advantages over time. You should also track your customers informally. Every evening, spend five minutes reviewing the day. Which products sold well? Which customers came? What did they ask for that you did not have? Write these down. After a month, you will see patterns. You will know which days are busy, which products are fast-moving, and which customers are regulars. This information is gold. It helps you order stock, set prices, and plan promotions. Consider doing a simple customer survey. You do not need a formal questionnaire. Just ask ten customers: what do you wish I stocked? What would make you come more often? What do you dislike about shopping here? Listen carefully. Do not argue. Thank them. Then act on the most common answers. Finally, think about inclusion. Your customer base includes people with different abilities, ages, and incomes. Can an elderly person reach your shelves? Can a person with a disability enter your shop? Can a mother with a baby find what she needs quickly? Small adjustments, such as lower shelves, wider entrances, and clear signage, can expand your market. In summary, knowing your customers means mapping your catchment, segmenting by needs, understanding payment behaviour, managing credit carefully, growing frequency and basket size, building trust, competing on reliability, tracking patterns, and including everyone. Do this consistently and your shop will not just survive; it will thrive. In the next lesson we will look at stock selection and supplier management, building on what you have learned about your customers.

lessons.title: Module 2 Lesson 2: Stock Selection and Supplier Management for Small Shops
lessons.body: In this lesson we turn to the goods you sell and the people you buy from. Stock selection and supplier management are the engine of your shop. If you stock the wrong items, you tie up cash and lose sales. If you manage suppliers poorly, you run out of fast-moving goods and pay too much. Across African markets, successful traders are ruthless about what they stock and disciplined about how they buy. Let us start with stock selection. The first principle is to stock what your customers actually buy, not what you like or what looks nice. Use the customer knowledge from Lesson 1. Make a list of your top 20 selling items. These are your core stock. Never run out of them. In a typical small shop in Africa, core items might include maize flour, rice, cooking oil, sugar, salt, tea leaves, milk, bread, soap, detergent, matches, candles, airtime, and mobile money float. Your specific list depends on your location and customers. The second principle is the 80/20 rule. Roughly 80 percent of your sales often come from 20 percent of your products. Identify that 20 percent and protect it. Do not spread your limited capital across too many slow-moving items. It is better to have deep stock of fast movers than shallow stock of everything. The third principle is to balance necessities and impulse items. Necessities are things people must buy regularly, such as food and soap. Impulse items are things people buy on a whim, such as sweets, biscuits, cold drinks, and small toys. Necessities bring customers in. Impulse items increase basket size. A good shop has both. The fourth principle is to consider shelf life and storage. In hot and humid conditions, some goods spoil quickly. Buy perishables in quantities you can sell before they expire. Use proper storage: keep flour and rice off the floor, keep soap away from food, keep cold drinks in a fridge or cooler, and protect goods from rats, insects, and moisture. If you sell fresh produce, plan for daily or every-other-day purchases. The fifth principle is to watch for seasonality. Demand changes with seasons, school terms, holidays, and festivals. During Ramadan, dates, milk, and sugar sell more. During Christmas and New Year, rice, cooking oil, and drinks sell more. During school opening, exercise books, pens, and uniforms sell more. During the rainy season, umbrellas, plastic bags, and waterproof items sell more. Plan your stock around these cycles. Now let us turn to supplier management. Your suppliers are your partners. Treat them well, but also hold them accountable. Start by identifying multiple suppliers for your core items. Do not rely on one supplier for everything. If that supplier raises prices, runs out, or delays delivery, your shop suffers. Having two or three suppliers for key products gives you options and bargaining power. When choosing a supplier, consider price, quality, reliability, distance, and payment terms. Price is important, but the cheapest supplier is not always the best. A slightly more expensive supplier who delivers on time and consistently provides good quality may be more profitable in the long run. Reliability means they have stock when you need it and deliver when they promise. Distance affects transport costs and delivery time. Payment terms matter because they affect your cash flow. Some suppliers offer credit for a week or a month. This can help you stock more without using all your cash. But do not abuse credit. Pay on time to build trust and secure better terms. Build relationships with suppliers. Visit their shops or warehouses. Learn their names. Understand their own pressures. If you are a reliable buyer who pays on time and orders consistently, you can negotiate better prices, priority during shortages, and sometimes free delivery. Do not always push for the lowest price. Sometimes a fair price with reliable supply is better than a rock-bottom price with unreliable supply. When you negotiate, be prepared. Know the market price. Know how much you need. Know your maximum price. Ask for bulk discounts if you can afford to buy in larger quantities. Ask about returns for damaged goods. Ask about delivery schedules. Get agreements in writing where possible, even if it is just a WhatsApp message confirming the order and price. This protects you if there is a dispute. Managing stock levels is a daily discipline. Use a simple stock card or notebook for each core item. Record when stock comes in, when it goes out, and the balance. If you have a smartphone, you can use a simple spreadsheet or a free inventory app. The goal is to know at a glance what you have and what you need to order. Set reorder points. A reorder point is the level at which you must order more stock to avoid running out before the next delivery. For example, if you sell 10 bags of maize flour per day and your supplier takes 2 days to deliver, you should reorder when you have 20 bags left, plus a safety buffer of maybe 5 bags. So your reorder point is 25 bags. Adjust based on how reliable your supplier is and how much storage you have. Conduct a stock count regularly. Weekly is good for most small shops. Monthly is the minimum. Count everything. Compare with your records. Investigate differences. Shrinkage, which is loss from theft, damage, or error, is a silent killer of small shops. Knowing your numbers helps you catch it early. Also watch for dead stock. Dead stock is inventory that has not sold in 30, 60, or 90 days. It ties up your cash and takes up space. Identify it. Try to sell it at a discount, bundle it with fast movers, or return it to the supplier if possible. Do not let dead stock sit forever. Learn from it. Why did it not sell? Was it the wrong product, wrong price, or wrong season? Avoid repeating the mistake. In African markets, transport and logistics are often challenging. Roads may be bad, fuel prices may fluctuate, and deliveries may be delayed. Build buffer stock for items that are critical and hard to restock quickly. But do not overstock perishables or items that may become obsolete, such as phone accessories that change with new models. Consider joining forces with other small shops to buy in bulk. A buying group or cooperative can negotiate better prices and share transport costs. This is common in some African markets and can significantly improve your margins. If you do this, set clear rules for ordering, payment, and distribution. Finally, think about ethical and legal sourcing. Buy from legitimate suppliers. Avoid counterfeit goods, expired products, and stolen goods. Not only is it illegal, but it destroys customer trust. If a customer gets sick from expired food or a fake phone charger damages their phone, they will never return, and they may tell others. Your reputation is your most valuable asset. In summary, stock selection and supplier management require discipline. Stock what customers buy, focus on fast movers, balance necessities and impulse items, manage shelf life and seasonality, use multiple suppliers, negotiate fairly, track stock levels, set reorder points, count regularly, clear dead stock, and source ethically. Do these things and your shop will have the right goods at the right time at the right price. In the next lesson we will focus on pricing and profit calculation, which builds directly on the stock and supplier decisions you make.

lessons.title: Module 2 Lesson 3: Pricing and Profit Calculation for Small Traders
lessons.body: Pricing is one of the most important decisions you make in your small shop or market stall. Price too high and customers go elsewhere. Price too low and you work hard for nothing. In this lesson we will cover how to calculate your costs, set prices that earn a profit, and adjust prices when conditions change. This is practical, business-first training for African traders. Let us start with the difference between cost, price, and profit. Cost is what you pay to acquire or produce the goods you sell. Price is what the customer pays you. Profit is what remains after you subtract all your costs from your sales revenue. Many small traders confuse revenue with profit. If you sell 100,000 shillings worth of goods in a day, that is revenue, not profit. Your profit is what is left after you pay for the goods, transport, rent, electricity, airtime, wages, and any other expenses. To price properly, you must know your costs. There are two types of costs: direct costs and indirect costs. Direct costs, also called cost of goods sold, are the costs directly tied to the products you sell. If you buy a bag of rice for 50,000 and sell it for 60,000, your direct cost is 50,000. Indirect costs, also called overheads or operating expenses, are costs that keep your shop running but are not tied to a specific item. These include rent, electricity, water, transport for restocking, phone airtime, packaging, wages, licenses, and taxes. You must cover both direct and indirect costs to make a true profit. A common mistake is to calculate profit only on the difference between buying and selling price, ignoring overheads. For example, you buy a crate of soda for 20,000 and sell it for 24,000. You think you made 4,000 profit. But if you paid 1,000 for transport, 500 for airtime to order, and a share of your daily rent is 1,500, your real profit is only 1,000. If you did not account for these, you might wrongly think you are doing well. So the first step in pricing is to calculate your true cost per item. Take the purchase price, add transport and handling costs, and then add a share of your overheads. For small shops, a simple way is to estimate your total monthly overheads and divide by the number of items you expect to sell in a month. This gives you an overhead cost per item. Add that to your direct cost to get your true cost. For example, if your monthly overheads are 300,000 and you sell 3,000 items per month, your overhead cost per item is 100. If you buy an item for 500, your true cost is 600. Now you can set a price above 600 to make a profit. The second step is to decide your profit margin. Profit margin is the percentage of the selling price that is profit. There are two common ways to calculate margin: markup on cost and margin on selling price. Markup on cost is the amount added to the cost, expressed as a percentage of cost. If your true cost is 600 and you sell for 750, your markup is 150, which is 25 percent of 600. Margin on selling price is profit divided by selling price. In this case, 150 divided by 750 is 20 percent. Both are useful, but be clear which one you are using. In many African markets, traders talk about markup. A common markup for fast-moving goods is 10 to 20 percent. For slower-moving or specialty goods, it may be 30 to 50 percent or more. Perishables may have higher markups because of spoilage risk. Airtime and mobile money float often have very thin margins, sometimes 2 to 5 percent, but they bring customers who buy other things. The third step is to consider what the market will bear. Your price must be acceptable to customers. If you set a price that is too high, they will buy from a competitor or substitute a different product. Do a simple price check. Walk around your market or neighborhood. See what others charge for similar goods. Note the quality and quantity. If your product is better or your shop is more convenient, you may charge a small premium. If your product is the same, you must be competitive. But do not start a price war. Competing only on price destroys everyone's profit. Instead, compete on service, reliability, and convenience. The fourth step is to use psychological pricing where appropriate. In many markets, prices ending in 9 or 5 are common. For example, 99 instead of 100, or 195 instead of 200. This is not just a Western idea; it works in many African markets too. However, in some contexts, round numbers are preferred for ease of change, especially where small coins are scarce. Know your customers. If they struggle to get change, round prices may be better. The fifth step is to review your prices regularly. Prices are not permanent. Your costs change. Inflation affects the price of goods. Fuel prices affect transport. Exchange rates affect imported goods. When your costs rise, you must adjust your prices, or your profit disappears. Do not wait too long. If you delay, you may sell at a loss for weeks before you realize it. Review your prices at least monthly. Keep a simple record of your purchase prices and selling prices. When a supplier raises prices, calculate your new true cost and decide on a new selling price. Communicate price changes clearly to customers. Use labels or a price list. If a customer complains, explain that your costs have gone up. Most customers understand, especially in inflationary environments. The sixth step is to calculate your break-even point. Break-even is the level of sales at which your total revenue equals your total costs, meaning you make no profit but no loss. Knowing your break-even helps you set sales targets. To calculate break-even in units, divide your total fixed costs by the profit per unit. Fixed costs are overheads that do not change with sales volume, such as rent. If your monthly fixed costs are 300,000 and your profit per item is 150, your break-even is 2,000 items per month. You must sell at least 2,000 items to cover your costs. Anything above that is profit. This is a powerful number to know. The seventh step is to manage discounts carefully. Discounts can attract customers, clear dead stock, and increase volume. But they also reduce your margin. Only discount if you still make a profit, or if you are deliberately clearing stock at a loss to recover cash. Do not discount your core fast-moving items regularly, because customers will wait for discounts and you will train them to expect lower prices. Instead, use discounts for slow movers, bulk purchases, or special promotions with a clear end date. The eighth step is to separate business and personal money. This is not strictly pricing, but it affects profit calculation. Many small traders mix cash. They take money from the till for personal use and then cannot tell if the business is profitable. Open a separate bank account or mobile money wallet for the business. Pay yourself a fixed salary or draw. Record all business income and expenses. This discipline will make your profit calculations accurate. Finally, let us consider a practical example. Amina runs a small shop in a market in Kampala. She sells sugar, rice, cooking oil, and soap. She buys a 5kg bag of sugar for 12,000. Transport adds 500 per bag. Her monthly overheads are 400,000, and she sells about 2,000 items per month, so overhead per item is 200. Her true cost for the sugar is 12,700. She decides on a 15 percent markup on cost, which is 1,905. She rounds the selling price to 15,000. Her profit per bag is 2,300. She sells about 200 bags of sugar per month, giving a profit of 460,000 from sugar alone. She does similar calculations for other products. She reviews prices monthly. When the price of sugar rises to 13,500, she recalculates and adjusts her selling price to 16,500, explaining to customers that supplier prices have gone up. In summary, pricing and profit calculation require you to know your true costs, choose a margin, check the market, use psychological pricing wisely, review regularly, calculate break-even, manage discounts, separate business and personal money, and practice with real numbers. Do this and you will not just be busy; you will be profitable. In the next lesson we will cover record keeping and cash flow management, which are essential for sustaining your profit.

lessons.title: Module 2 Lesson 4: Record Keeping and Cash Flow Management
lessons.body: In this lesson we focus on the financial discipline that separates thriving small shops from those that close within a year: record keeping and cash flow management. Across Africa, many small traders run their businesses from memory. They know roughly what they bought, roughly what they sold, and roughly what they have. But roughly is not enough. Without records, you cannot know your true profit, you cannot plan, and you cannot access credit or grow. Without cash flow management, you may be profitable on paper but still run out of cash to buy stock. Let us start with record keeping. You do not need complicated accounting. You need simple, consistent records that you actually use. There are five basic records every small shop should keep. First, a sales record. This can be a notebook where you write daily sales totals. If you sell on credit, record each credit sale separately with the customer name, item, amount, and date. If you have a smartphone, you can use a simple spreadsheet or a free app. The key is to record every sale, even small ones. Second, a purchase record. Record every purchase: date, supplier, item, quantity, unit price, total cost, and whether you paid cash or credit. This helps you track your cost of goods and know what you owe. Third, an expense record. Record all business expenses: rent, electricity, water, transport, airtime, wages, licenses, taxes, packaging, and repairs. Keep receipts where possible. If you cannot get a receipt, write the details in your notebook. Fourth, a stock record. As covered in Lesson 2, keep a stock card or list for your core items. Record stock in, stock out, and balance. This helps you prevent theft and avoid running out. Fifth, a cash book. This is a daily record of money coming in and money going out. It shows your cash position. At the end of each day, count your cash and compare it with your cash book. If there is a difference, investigate. Do not ignore it. Now, why is record keeping so important? First, it tells you your true profit. You can calculate revenue minus cost of goods minus expenses. Without records, you are guessing. Second, it helps you make decisions. Which products are most profitable? Which customers owe you money? Which expenses are rising? Records answer these questions. Third, it helps you access credit. If you want a loan from a bank, microfinance institution, or mobile money lender, they will ask for records. Even informal lenders want to see that you are organized. Fourth, it helps you plan. You can forecast sales, plan purchases, and set targets. Fifth, it protects you. If a customer claims they paid but you have no record, you may lose money. If a supplier claims you owe more than you do, your records protect you. Let us talk about how to keep records when you are busy. The best time to record is immediately after the transaction. Keep a notebook and pen at the counter. If you use a phone, keep the app open. Do not wait until evening, because you will forget details. If you have staff, train them to record sales and expenses. Do spot checks. Make it clear that records are not optional. At the end of each day, spend 10 to 15 minutes updating your records and counting cash. At the end of each week, review your sales, expenses, and stock. At the end of each month, calculate your profit and loss. This monthly review is powerful. It shows you trends and helps you adjust. Now let us turn to cash flow management. Cash flow is the movement of money in and out of your business. Profit is not the same as cash flow. You can be profitable but have no cash if customers owe you money, if you have too much stock, or if you spent cash on personal items. Cash flow problems are a major reason small shops fail. To manage cash flow, you must understand your cash cycle. The cash cycle is the time between when you pay for stock and when you receive cash from selling it. If you buy stock on Monday and sell it by Friday, your cash cycle is five days. If you buy on credit and pay after 30 days, but sell within a week, your cash cycle is negative, which is good because you receive cash before you pay. If you buy on cash but sell slowly, your cash cycle is long, which strains your cash. To improve cash flow, you can negotiate longer payment terms with suppliers, reduce the time it takes to sell stock, collect receivables faster, and manage your expenses carefully. Let us look at practical strategies. First, forecast your cash flow. At the start of each week, estimate how much cash you will receive from sales and credit collections, and how much you will pay for stock, rent, wages, and other expenses. If you see a shortfall coming, act early. You can delay a purchase, negotiate a payment extension, or reduce expenses. Second, manage credit sales carefully. As mentioned in Lesson 1, credit can build loyalty but can also kill your cash flow. Set clear credit limits. Follow up on overdue payments politely but firmly. Use mobile money reminders or WhatsApp messages. If a customer consistently pays late, stop offering credit. Third, manage your stock levels. Too much stock ties up cash. Too little stock loses sales. Use the reorder points from Lesson 2. Aim for a balance. For fast movers, keep enough stock to avoid running out. For slow movers, keep minimal stock. Fourth, separate business and personal cash. This is critical. If you mix cash, you will never know your true cash position. Pay yourself a fixed amount. Do not take money from the till for personal needs without recording it as a draw. Better yet, transfer a fixed salary to your personal mobile money or bank account. Fifth, build a cash reserve. Save a small amount every week. Even 500 or 1,000 shillings per day adds up. Keep this reserve for emergencies, such as a sudden price increase, a broken fridge, or a medical emergency. A cash reserve prevents you from borrowing at high interest or selling stock at a loss. Sixth, use mobile money wisely. Mobile money is convenient but it has fees. If you receive payments via mobile money, factor in the withdrawal fees. If you send money, compare fees. Sometimes it is cheaper to use a bank transfer or cash. Also, be careful with mobile money fraud. Do not share your PIN. Confirm payments before releasing goods. Keep a record of mobile money transactions. Seventh, manage debt. If you have loans, know the repayment schedule. Pay on time to avoid penalties and protect your creditworthiness. Do not take new loans to pay old loans unless you have a clear plan. If you are struggling, talk to your lender early. Many lenders prefer to restructure than to write off a loan. Eighth, review your cash flow weekly. Look at your cash book. Are you collecting more than you spend? If not, why? Are there expenses you can cut? Are there customers who owe you too much? Are you overstocking? Make adjustments. Let us consider a practical example. Chidi runs a small shop in Enugu, Nigeria. He sells provisions and phone accessories. He used to mix business and personal money. He often ran out of cash to buy stock, even though he was selling well. He started keeping a cash book. He discovered that he was taking about 20,000 naira per week for personal use without recording it. He also had 50,000 naira in unpaid customer credit. He set a personal salary of 10,000 naira per week. He followed up on credit and collected 30,000 naira. He reduced his stock of slow-moving phone cases and used the cash to buy more fast-moving recharge cards and drinks. Within two months, his cash flow improved. He was able to pay suppliers on time and even save a small reserve. In summary, record keeping and cash flow management are the backbone of a sustainable small shop. Keep sales, purchase, expense, stock, and cash records. Review them daily, weekly, and monthly. Manage your cash cycle, forecast cash flow, control credit, manage stock, separate business and personal money, build a reserve, use mobile money wisely, manage debt, and review weekly. Do these things and you will have the financial control to grow. In the next lesson we will cover customer service, marketing, and growth strategies for small shops and market traders.

lessons.title: Module 2 Lesson 5: Customer Service, Marketing, and Growth Strategies
lessons.body: In this final lesson of Module 2, we bring together everything you have learned about customers, stock, pricing, and records, and apply it to customer service, marketing, and growth. In competitive African markets, good customer service and smart marketing can be the difference between a shop that survives and one that thrives. Growth does not always mean opening a second shop. It can mean increasing sales in your current shop, adding new products, or serving new customer segments. Let us start with customer service. Customer service is how you treat people before, during, and after a sale. In small shops and market stalls, it is personal. Customers can choose from many sellers. They will return to the one who makes them feel respected and valued. Good customer service starts with greeting. Greet every customer warmly, even if they are just passing. Use local languages where appropriate. A simple hello, welcome, or how are you can open the door to a sale. Next, be attentive. Listen to what the customer asks for. Do not interrupt. If you do not have what they want, offer an alternative or tell them when you will have it. If you promise to get it, keep your promise. Next, be efficient. Customers value their time. Know your prices. Know where items are. Be quick at the counter. If there is a queue, acknowledge waiting customers and apologize for delays. If you can, open a second till or have a staff member help. Next, be honest. Do not sell expired or damaged goods. Do not overcharge. If a customer asks for a product you do not have, do not pretend you do. If you make a mistake, apologize and correct it. Honesty builds long-term trust. Next, handle complaints well. Complaints are opportunities to improve. Listen without arguing. Thank the customer for telling you. If you are wrong, fix it. If you are not wrong, explain politely. Do not lose your temper. A customer whose complaint is handled well often becomes more loyal than one who never complained. Next, show appreciation. Thank customers for their business. A small thank you, a smile, or a greeting by name goes a long way. quiz.q: What is the main purpose of tracking daily sales in a small shop?
options: A) To know exactly how much cash is in the till at closing
B) To identify which products sell best and make better buying decisions
C) To calculate the shop rent automatically
D) To replace the need for a business license
quiz.explanation: Tracking daily sales helps a trader see which items move quickly and which do not, so buying and pricing decisions improve.

quiz.q: Which pricing method adds a fixed percentage to the cost of an item?
options: A) Loss leader pricing
B) Penetration pricing
C) Markup pricing
D) Bundle pricing
quiz.explanation: Markup pricing sets the selling price by adding a set percentage to the cost price of the item.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep a simple record of stock levels in a market stall?
options: A) To prevent running out of fast selling items and avoid overstocking slow ones
B) To increase the number of customers automatically
C) To avoid paying tax on unsold goods
D) To make suppliers give free goods
quiz.explanation: Stock records show what needs restocking and what is sitting too long, which protects cash flow and reduces waste.

quiz.q: What does a cash flow problem usually mean for a small trader?
options: A) The trader has too many customers
B) The trader has no suppliers
C) The trader has too much stock
D) The trader cannot pay bills on time even if sales are good
quiz.explanation: Cash flow problems happen when money going out is more than money coming in at the right time, making it hard to pay bills.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good way to handle customer complaints in a market setting?
options: A) Listen calmly, apologize, and offer a fair solution quickly
B) Argue until the customer leaves
C) Ignore the complaint and serve the next person
D) Raise the price for that customer next time
quiz.explanation: Handling complaints calmly and fairly builds trust and encourages customers to return and recommend the stall.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to calculate gross profit for a trading day?
options: A) Total sales minus total expenses including rent
B) Total sales minus the cost of goods sold
C) Total cash in the till minus personal spending
D) Total stock value plus total sales
quiz.explanation: Gross profit is sales revenue minus the direct cost of the goods that were sold.

quiz.q: Why should a small trader separate business money from personal money?
options: A) To impress the bank manager
B) To avoid paying suppliers
C) To know the true profit and loss of the business
D) To qualify for free stock
quiz.explanation: Separating money makes it clear whether the business is actually making a profit or losing money.

quiz.q: Which action best helps a market trader build repeat customers?
options: A) Changing location every day
B) Selling only the cheapest items
C) Keeping prices secret until asked
D) Offering consistent quality and friendly service
